resources.title: Artificial Intelligence
resources.summary: Artificial intelligence studies and builds systems that perform tasks associated with learning, inference, perception, and language. Its connection to human experience raises questions about knowledge, agency, and understanding.
subject: Artificial Intelligence

resources.title: Consciousness
resources.summary: Consciousness names the subjective dimension of experience: what it is like to perceive, think, and be aware. Whether and how this could relate to machine systems remains an open philosophical and scientific question.

resources.title: Memory

resources.title: Language

resources.title: What makes an experience conscious?
resources.summary: Which conditions or processes distinguish a conscious experience from information that is processed without being experienced.
resources.scope: Editorial scope note: this question is about the conditions of consciousness. Why experience exists at all is treated separately in Q002.
understand: The question asks what it is that makes some mental states conscious, as opposed to states that are processed without being experienced. This is an editorial framing; the sources below approach it through competing scientific theories.

It can be read in different ways. One reading asks which brain processes accompany consciousness and where and when they occur, which is how the adversarial collaborations below frame it. Another asks why any physical process is accompanied by experience at all; that reading is treated in Q002.
resources.statusJustification: Contested: the review by Seth and Bayne reports disagreement about what the theories require, and a letter about IIT shows disagreement over its scientific status (as reported by Scientific American). Active: a preregistered adversarial collaboration between proponents of GNWT and IIT has been designed and reported (Melloni et al. 2023; Cogitate Consortium 2025). Editorial judgment, subject to review.
openProblems: Whether current theories can be empirically distinguished.
Whether results about visual consciousness extend to other kinds of experience.
subject: Consciousness
Cognition

resources.title: Why does subjective experience exist?
resources.summary: Why physical processes in a brain, or any system, should be accompanied by experience from a point of view.
resources.scope: Editorial scope note: this is primarily a philosophical question. The sources read are philosophical arguments, not experiments, and this entry does not claim an experiment could settle it.
understand: The question asks why experience exists, as distinct from asking which brain processes accompany it (Q001). It is usually discussed as a problem in philosophy of mind.

Two interpretations are separated in the sources read. One treats experience as something reductive explanation could in principle capture; the other argues that reductive approaches leave out the core of the problem.
resources.statusJustification: Open: the sources read present this as a standing philosophical problem (Nagel 1974; Chalmers 1995), and none of them reports a resolution. This is an editorial judgment from a small set of sources, subject to review.
openProblems: Whether reductive explanation can account for subjective character.
subject: Consciousness

resources.title: Can consciousness be measured objectively?
resources.summary: Whether the presence, content, or neural basis of consciousness can be assessed by methods that do not rely only on a subject's report or on one theory.
resources.scope: Editorial scope note: the sources read focus on identifying neural correlates of consciousness. They do not establish a measure of consciousness itself.
understand: 'Measured objectively' can mean different things: detecting whether a system is conscious, quantifying how conscious it is, or identifying the neural processes that accompany reported experience. The sources read address the third; this entry does not claim the first two have a method.
Even the third depends on how conscious and non-conscious trials are identified and on which theory's predictions are being tested.
resources.statusJustification: Active: preregistered multi-method studies aimed at neural correlates have been designed and reported (Melloni et al. 2023; Cogitate Consortium 2025). Contested: whether current theories can be empirically distinguished is described as unclear (Seth and Bayne 2022), and the scientific status of IIT is disputed (as reported by Scientific American). Editorial judgment, subject to review.
openProblems: Which methods, if any, measure consciousness independently of theory.
Whether findings from visual tasks generalize.

resources.title: Can an artificial system genuinely understand meaning?
resources.summary: Whether a computational system can have understanding, as opposed to producing outputs that look as if it does.
resources.scope: Editorial scope note: the sources read include a philosophical argument, a proposed behavioral test, and a report of language-model performance. They are different kinds of material and do not answer the question together.
understand: The question asks whether an artificial system can understand what its inputs and outputs mean, or only manipulate them. It is separated here from the behavioral question in Q012 (is imitation sufficient evidence?) and the consciousness question in Q009.
Searle's term for what he says is missing is intentionality; Turing's approach sets aside the word 'think' in favor of behavior in a game.
resources.statusJustification: Contested: Searle argues programs alone cannot suffice for intentionality, while Turing proposed replacing the question with an imitation game. The performance report on GPT-3 describes capabilities and does not itself claim understanding. Editorial judgment, subject to review.
openProblems: Whether any behavior could demonstrate understanding.
Which later responses to Searle and Turing bear on current systems.

resources.title: What would count as evidence of machine consciousness?
resources.summary: What observations, if any, should lead us to attribute consciousness to an artificial system.
resources.scope: Editorial scope note: the main source read is a preprint abstract proposing one approach; this entry presents it as that, not as a settled method.
understand: The question asks what evidence would justify saying that an artificial system is conscious. It depends on what consciousness is taken to be (Q001) and on whether behavior is good evidence (Q012).
One published approach takes leading neuroscientific theories as a starting point and asks what computational properties each would require.
resources.statusJustification: Active: Butlin et al. propose assessing AI systems against indicator properties derived from scientific theories. Contested: the theories the indicators come from are themselves in dispute (Seth and Bayne 2022; Cogitate Consortium 2025). This is an editorial judgment, subject to review.
openProblems: Whether indicator approaches can be validated.

resources.title: Theories of consciousness
resources.summary: Reviews four approaches: higher-order theories, global workspace theories, re-entry and predictive processing theories, and integrated information theory. For each it covers what the theory aims to explain, its neurobiological commitments, and the evidence offered for it. It then considers how empirical debates might distinguish the theories and outlines three ways theories need to develop for rigorous testing.

resources.limitations: Only the abstract-level description was read for this preview; section-level characterizations of each theory were not read.

resources.title: Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: Formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms
resources.summary: Presents the current formulation of IIT. It lists a zeroth axiom (experience exists) and five essential properties of experience: intrinsicality, information, integration, exclusion, and composition. Each is translated into a postulate about the physical substrate, which must have cause-effect power, act within itself, select a specific cause-effect state, form an irreducible whole, be bounded by a maximal set of units, and specify a structured cause-effect profile. The paper states that these conditions are…
resources.read: Open-access full text retrieved and summarized.
resources.limitations: Authored by proponents. The authors state that the formal examples use small simulated networks, that the completeness of the axioms rests on introspection and reasoning, and that alternative candidate properties are conceivable.
resources.attribution: The Unanswered Archive; The Theory Chamber

Q001.limit: Presented as the theory's proponents' account.

Q003.finding: Presents the current formulation of IIT. It lists a zeroth axiom (experience exists) and five essential properties of experience: intrinsicality, information, integration, exclusion, and composition. Each is translated into a postulate about the physical substrate, which must have cause-effect power, act within itself, select a specific cause-effect state, form an irreducible whole, be bounded by a maximal set of units, and specify a structured cause-effect profile. The paper states that these conditions are necessary and sufficient for consciousness, that IIT yields testable predictions (some already tested), and that the formalism is still a work in progress.

Q001 asks which conditions make an experience conscious; Q002 asks why experience exists at all. They are separable questions about the same phenomenon.
Deciding how to measure consciousness depends on a view of what makes an experience conscious.
Both concern neural processes associated with conscious experience.
Both turn on the difference between conscious and unconscious processing.
Several theories relate attention and awareness, and some treat them as dissociable.
Whether consciousness is fundamental or emergent bears on what could make an experience conscious.
Self-awareness is one of the things a theory of consciousness may or may not need to explain.
Both ask whether physical explanation can be sufficient for consciousness.
Indicators for machine consciousness draw on theories whose empirical tests are contested.
Identifying necessary neural processes relies on the same experimental designs.
Whether consciousness depends on a biological substrate relates to whether it is fundamental or emergent.
Evidence of machine consciousness presupposes some view on whether non-biological systems could be conscious.
Whether intelligence needs consciousness and whether systems understand meaning are often argued together.
Separating intelligence from consciousness shapes what counts as evidence of the latter.
Both ask what consciousness adds to intelligent processing.
Both ask which capacities intelligence depends on.
Both ask whether behavior is enough to attribute understanding.
What counts as understanding and what counts as consciousness are often confused and sometimes linked.
Evaluating claims of artificial awareness requires the kind of evidence Q009 asks about.
Self-modeling features in several theory-derived indicators.
Self-representation and self-awareness are closely related concepts.
Self-representation may or may not be required for intelligence.
Both ask about the relationship between reasoning and other capacities.
How far machine reasoning resembles human reasoning bears on how responsibility is assigned.
Attention is often invoked in distinguishing conscious from unconscious processing.
Both concern the neural basis of conscious versus unconscious processing.
A continuous sense of self relates to self-awareness.
Memory and the sense of self are linked in discussions of identity.
Both ask how identity depends on memory.
Digital preservation of identity raises the same question about what memory contributes.
Both ask what preserving a person through records would involve.
Both concern what artificial or digital records can reproduce of remembering.
Which functions of memory matter for identity is relevant to what artificial memory must reproduce.
Altered or lost memory bears on the construction of a continuous self.
Moral consideration depends on how claims about artificial awareness can be evaluated.
Some views link moral consideration to evidence of consciousness.
Both ask how responsibility and moral standing are assigned to or around artificial systems.
